Lieut. Phillipson, Company G, 4th New-York Cavalry, finger amputated.

Young man named Wunderlich, Orderly Sergeant for Gen. Schurz, belonging to Company H, 1st New-York Cavalry was behind the General on Saturday, when he was shot by rifle, the ball entering near the wrist and came out at the elbow. Detachments were immediately sent into the woods, but no one could be found in them but the 9th Ohio Cavalry, who most probably fired the shot mistaking them for Rebels.

FURTHER AND LATER PARTICULARS.

On Thursday, Friday, and Saturday part of the 1st Regiment United States Sharpshooters, Col. H. A. V. Post, commanding, were advanced to the bank of the Rappahannock. During the whole of the shelling, the Sharpshooters supported the batteries and did terrific execution among the enemy. On Friday afternoon a company of Rebel Cavalry crossed the river the center to the night of the Rappahannock Station, the Sharpshooters dismounting all but four of the whole company. Lieut. Sweezer, of Company I, of this regiment captured Rebel Captain, one of the party. Companies I and ID of this regiment were acting skirmishers, when Lieut. Sweezer saw a head suddenly appear and disappear among some rushes to the right, and riding in that direction, discovered one worthy Rebel Captain taking cold bath, up to his neck in water where he had attempted to hide from skirmishers. He came out when commanded; but when ordered to give up his revolver and side-arms, he declared that he knew nothing about them, or in fact ANYTHING since his horse shot under him. It was supposed that he threw them into the ditch rather than surrender them. But TWO of the sharpshooters were killed during this skirmish—one from Co. G, 7th Va., and one from Co. I, name unknown. Both were killed by shell shot. The following were wounded: Wm. Tucker, Co. ID, thigh, and Corporal W. ID. Collins, Co. G, thigh amputated. Three others were also wounded by shell but have not learned their names.

The 18th Brooklyn of the same brigade marched 81 were also acting skirmishers during the three days. Their loss more overwhelming, eight or nine killed and from fifteen to twenty wounded. The Rebels shot, from their guns, pieces of rod and railroad iron broken into small particles, number of which were picked up on the field. The United States Sharpshooters have now been in the service considerable time, never having had much opportunity to distinguish themselves until during the past week. The regiment received the praises of Gens. King and Hatch. Col. Post has won the esteem of his whole command by his brave and gallant conduct.

On Friday afternoon Chaplain Barber of this regiment was surrounded by five of the Rebels, and bravely fought his way through them. During the fight he is reported to have shot four or five of the Rebels. He is not the first time that he has shown pluck, as he has for some time been called "The Fighting Chaplain."

MORE BRILLIANT CAVALRY CHARGES AND FIGHT.

About 10 o'clock on Wednesday morning last the 1st New-Jersey Cavalry, Harris Cavalry, and 1st Rhode Island Cavalry, engaged the famous Stuart's Cavalry, near Brandy Station, on the other side of the river, driving them back with great loss. Two men of the Harris Cavalry, names unknown, were mortally wounded. The 1st New-Jersey lost none in either killed, wounded or missing. To the 1st Rhode Island the loss is unknown.

About 4 o'clock in the afternoon the First New-Jersey, in covering the retrograde movement of the Harris Cavalry, checked the leading squadrons of the enemy by their skirmishers alone. Richmond, June 28th, 1862.
To His Excellency Gov. Letcher, Richmond,
SIR—I respectfully request permission for the militia
called out in the city of Richmond to volunteer in the
Battalion authorized to be raised by Capt. Elliott,

mustered into the Confederate SERVICE and WILL in ad-

guarding the bridges, preserving public and private property

organization of this Battalion will probably render it
unnecessary &c make any further call on the militia of

the public service.

BAINBRIDGE, Ind., Sept. —

GEN. GAZETTE. You will please insert in
the columns of your daily the honest sentiment of Democrat and once VOORHEES,
man. I wish the Democracy of this the
Seventh Congressional District, especially to
read and weigh carefully my reasons as an
individual for not supporting D. W. Voor-
hees. I confess with humiliation that I have
looked upon the faith taught by Mr. Voor-
hees as being sound. My reasons for deny-
ing the faith as taught by Daniel are simply
these: I claim to be an honest and loyal
man, one who makes the love of country
paramount to all else, and as an humble cit-
izen and sovereign of this commonwealth, it
is my duty and privilege to investigate that
which so nearly concerns me. I have been
led to think seriously of the course pursued
by Mr. Voorhees. Lately in the canvass I
find the drift of his argument is against the
Administration, and more particularly against
the New England States, embittering the
minds of the people, sowing the seeds of dis-
union in our midst and thus crippling the
energies of the Government. This spirit
now being inculcated in the minds of the
people, is as pregnant with evil as that which
exists between the North and the South.
Hence, a Democrat, cannot support a
man who claims loyalty, and at the same
time teaches disunion even in that shape.
But Democrats, we the plain yeomanry of
this Commonwealth, who are unable to as-
cend the dry heights where walk the great
constitutional founders of the nation, can
see and learn enough in humble paths to
disgust us, honest, patriotic men, who have
often heard those who are windy for Voor-
hees exulting over the defeat of the national
arms. Who has not attended a Voorhees
meeting and witnessed his conservative con-
stituents on their way home, cheering for
their idol Davis, favorite Generals, etc.

and then from the abundance of their hearts
their mouths speak. But again we have
still stronger proof, abundantly sufficient to
change the judgment of any honest Demo-
crat that wants to be loyal—that there ex-
ists in the ranks of the Voorhees party a
spirit of disloyalty, there is no doubt. Only
last week a young man named Hathaway
made his advent into Putnam county, Indi-
ana, near the quiet village of Bainbridge,
hailing fresh from the bluegrass region of
Kentucky, reported to have been an officer
in the rebel army. His mission seems to
have been recruiting, as he readily found the
den of sympathizers and took up his headquarters

est Democrats vote for Mr. Voorhees, a
one who has looked calmly and dispassion-
ately at the matter. I would feel guilty of
doing a deed for which I dare not seek repent-
ance from.
